To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the glycosylation patterns in HCV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma differ from those in liver metastasis of colonic carcinoma and colorectal carcinoma.
the changes in the glycosylations of haptoglobin, hemoglobin and complement factor H, quantified by MRM and FTICR, can differentiate HCC of viral etiology from liver metastasis of CRC and CRC.
the glycosylation profiles of three plasma proteins are altered in HCC of HVC etiology and that these alterations can be quantitatively determined by two LC-MS workflows.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of analytical methods for the determination of glycopeptides in biological matrices, and their use in the study of changes in glycosylation in HCC, and colorectal cancer.
the development of new tools for quantitative analysis of glycopeptides in biological samples.
the use of LC-MS methods for the analysis of the changes in the glycosylated forms of serum proteins, which may serve as biomarkers in HCC and colorectal cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both workflows allow accurate relative quantification of N- and/or O-glycopeptidic species.
the two workflows provide complementary information and that the two approaches are suitable for the quantification of glycoproteins in complex biological samples.
both methods are adequate for relative quantitation of glycopeptides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of MRM or full MS scan FT-ICRs is a viable approach for the relative quantification of specific glycopeptide ratios and the results can provide useful information on the glycosylation changes in cancer samples.
both LC-MS workflows can be used for relative quantification of specific glycopeptide species and that the full-MS scan mode of FT-ICR can be used for this purpose.
the use of full-MS scan in FT-ICR allows for the quantification of glycoprotein glycoforms, and that MRM is more suited for quantification of a specific glycoform.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LC-MS based glycoproteomics can be successfully applied to the analysis of cancer samples.
LC-MS methods can be used to quantify glycopeptides in clinical samples and that the results are consistent with those obtained using other methods.
both workflows can be used for quantification of glycoprotein expression.
